result: As of September 2022, there is a stark global vaccine inequity: 80% of citizens in low-income countries are still waiting for their first COVID-19 vaccine dose, while almost 80% of citizens in high-income countries are vaccinated. In the past 12 months, high-income countries administered almost 100 doses per 100 people compared to only 27 in low-income countries.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 provide consistent descriptive statistics about global vaccine inequity with proper citations to data sources (Mathieu et al., 2021; Our World in Data, 2022). The claims are internally consistent and represent factual reporting of vaccination rates at a specific time point.

result: Unequal vaccine distribution has ethical consequences, leading to high transmission, severe infections, and deaths in regions with lowest healthcare capacity, thereby aggravating health inequities between Global South and North. A modeling study found that if the 50 richest countries used all available vaccines, this would lead to twice as many COVID-19 deaths compared to proportional allocation.
evaluation: Claims C4-C6 present ethical arguments supported by appropriate citations. C6 specifically cites a modeling study (Herzog et al., 2021) providing quantitative evidence. The claims are logically consistent and properly attributed to prior work.

result: Constrained vaccine access in LMICs would reduce global GDP by US$153 billion annually, including US$56 billion loss in the EU and US combined. Every dollar spent on supplying vaccines to LMICs would yield a return of US$4.8.
evaluation: Claims C7-C9 cite economic estimates from the RAND Corporation (Hafner et al., 2020) with specific numerical values. The claims are internally consistent and properly attributed, though they represent estimates from a single source rather than empirical findings from this study.

result: Unmitigated COVID-19 transmissions in some parts of the world create evolutionary reservoirs from which new SARS-CoV-2 variants arise, increasing the risk of immune escape for both vaccine-induced and natural immunity.
evaluation: Claims C10-C11 present virological arguments supported by multiple citations (Saad-Roy et al., 2021; Telenti et al., 2021; van Oosterhout et al., 2021; Wagner et al., 2021). The claims represent established scientific understanding about viral evolution and are appropriately attributed.

result: The globally unequal vaccine distribution is partly due to vaccine nationalism in high-income countries. Several governments made bilateral purchasing agreements outside of COVAX, weakening its collective purchasing power. Substantial proportions of announced donations (25% of EU doses, almost 50% of US doses) have not yet been delivered.
evaluation: Claims C12-C15 describe the political and institutional context of vaccine distribution with appropriate citations. The specific data about undelivered donations (C14-C15) are cited to WHO and Our World in Data sources. The claims are factually consistent and properly attributed.

result: Prior studies on COVID-19 vaccine allocation preferences examined prioritization within high-income countries during vaccine scarcity, revealing support for prioritizing healthcare workers and vulnerable groups. Limited prior work examined cross-border allocation preferences, with mixed findings. No previous study exclusively sampled unvaccinated participants willing to be vaccinated.
evaluation: Claims C17-C25 provide a comprehensive literature review with appropriate citations. The claims accurately summarize prior work and identify the novelty of the current study (C25). The review is balanced and properly attributed to specific studies.

result: The German survey was launched at the height of the third wave in April 2021, while the other five surveys were carried out in June 2021, coinciding with a phase of low case numbers in each country.
evaluation: Claims C26-C27 describe the timing of data collection with reference to Figure 1 showing COVID-19 case data. The claims are factual statements about study design that are verifiable from the provided figure.

result: Discrete choice experiments (DCEs) measure the relative importance of different characteristics in decision-making. DCEs are based on random utility theory and have advantages over other stated preference techniques including mimicking real-world scenarios, reducing cognitive complexity, and eliciting implicit preferences.
evaluation: Claims C28-C30 describe the DCE methodology with appropriate citations (Mangham et al., 2009; Hall et al., 2004). The claims accurately represent established methodological knowledge and are properly attributed.

result: Participants were eligible only if unvaccinated and willing to be vaccinated. Power calculations indicated an optimal sample size of n=2,061 per country, but this was only reached in Germany due to timing and budget constraints. Sample sizes in other countries ranged from 670 (Poland) to 925 (Spain), totaling 6,030 eligible responses.
evaluation: Claims C31-C34 describe study eligibility criteria and sample sizes with appropriate citation for power calculations (de Bekker-Grob et al., 2015). The authors transparently acknowledge not meeting target sample sizes in most countries and provide clear justification.

result: In France, Italy, Spain, and Sweden, respondents on average chose candidates from the Global South over candidates from their own country (ORs: 1.37-1.79, all p<0.001). German respondents showed the opposite pattern (OR: 0.69, p<0.001). In Poland, country of residence had no significant effect (OR: 0.99).
evaluation: Claims C35-C41 present the main DCE results with specific odds ratios, confidence intervals, and p-values. The statistical results are clearly reported and internally consistent. The findings are supported by Table 3 in the manuscript.

result: In all six countries, candidates with increased COVID-19 mortality risk had 2-6 times higher odds of being chosen for vaccination. The effect was even more pronounced for strongly increased mortality risk (OR: 4.35 in Poland to OR: 14.20 in Sweden, all p<0.001).
evaluation: Claims C42-C43 present consistent findings across all countries regarding mortality risk as a key driver of vaccine allocation preferences. The results are clearly reported with specific ranges and statistical significance, supported by Table 3.

result: In all countries, employed candidates who lost income due to the pandemic and those employed in essential services were significantly more likely to be chosen for vaccination compared to unemployed candidates. Additionally, 40-year-old candidates had slightly higher odds of being chosen than 20- or 60-year-old candidates.
evaluation: Claims C44-C45 present consistent patterns across countries for employment status and age effects. The findings are supported by Table 3 showing statistically significant effects across countries, though the magnitude varies.

result: In the pooled heterogeneity analysis, female (OR: 1.22, p<0.001) and more educated respondents (OR: 1.63, p<0.001) were more likely to choose Global South candidates, while older respondents (OR: 0.68, p<0.001) and those at high COVID-19 risk (OR: 0.70, p<0.001) were less likely. Employed respondents showed slightly lower support (OR: 0.89, p=0.045). Threat perception had no significant effect (p=0.071).
evaluation: Claims C46-C51 present heterogeneity analysis results with specific odds ratios, confidence intervals, and p-values. The results are clearly reported and supported by Figure 3 and supplementary files. The statistical analysis appears appropriate for the data.

result: Respondents living in regions with higher COVID-19 case incidence were on average slightly less supportive of distributing vaccines to Global South candidates (OR: 0.998, 95% CI: 0.997-0.998, p<0.001).
evaluation: Claim C52 presents subnational heterogeneity analysis results with specific statistics. While the effect size is very small (OR: 0.998), it is highly statistically significant. The analysis is supported by Figure 5 and supplementary files showing regional COVID-19 data.

result: Vaccine allocation preferences are largely driven by assessed vulnerability of recipients, irrespective of country of residence. Respondents prioritize candidates with higher mortality risk even if they have foreign nationality, and prioritize based on employment status and income losses due to the pandemic.
evaluation: Claims C53-C55 present interpretations of the DCE results that are well-supported by the statistical findings (C35-C45). The interpretation that vulnerability drives preferences is consistent with the strong effects of mortality risk and employment status across countries.

result: Studies have found in-group bias in distributional preferences, but cross-country analyses found German citizens to be among the least nationalistic in Europe and not outliers in terms of altruism or pro-sociality.
evaluation: Claims C56-C58 cite relevant literature to contextualize the unexpected German findings. The citations (Bernhard et al., 2006; Reese et al., 2012; Yudkin et al., 2016; Coenders et al., 2021; Lubbers and Coenders, 2017; Fehr et al., 2021) are appropriate and the claims accurately represent prior work.

result: When surveys were fielded in Italy, France, Spain, Poland, and Sweden, vaccination rates exceeded 50% for first doses, whereas in Germany it was only 25%. The differential German findings are most likely driven by a combination of higher infection rates, lower vaccination rates, and a higher proportion of older, high-risk, and lower educated respondents in the German sample.
evaluation: Claims C59-C61 provide contextual data about vaccination rates and offer a plausible explanation for the German findings. The interpretation (C61) is supported by the heterogeneity analyses (C46-C49) showing that older, high-risk, and less educated respondents were less supportive of Global South allocation.

result: The samples are not nationally representative due to eligibility criteria (unvaccinated and willing to be vaccinated). The estimates of support for global solidarity are most likely lower bound estimates, assuming already vaccinated citizens would be even more willing to donate vaccine doses.
evaluation: Claim C62 accurately acknowledges a limitation regarding sample representativeness. However, C63's assertion that estimates are lower bounds is speculative and lacks empirical support. The assumption that vaccinated individuals would be more supportive of donations is plausible but unverified.

result: The WHO's call for a moratorium on booster vaccinations went unheeded. The emergence of Omicron emphasizes the transboundary nature of COVID-19. Governments of European countries can rely on solid public approval for equitable vaccine distribution, especially among female, younger, and more educated citizens. Public support may be even more pronounced now that risk groups have received boosters.
evaluation: Claims C64-C69 present policy implications and conclusions based on the study findings. C64-C65 provide factual context with appropriate citations. C66 is a reasonable conclusion supported by the DCE results (C35-C39, C46-C48). C67 is speculative but clearly presented as such. C68-C69 extend the findings to policy recommendations, which are appropriately framed as implications rather than empirical findings.
